Anchor Constraints

In this notebook, we show how to use an anchor constraint, which lets us pin some of the embedding vectors to specific values. This can be useful if you know a priori what some of the embedding vectors should be. Below, we'll use an anchor constraint when laying out a binary tree: we'll pin the leaves to lie on a circle.
This next cell constraints a binary tree with a specified depth. You can change the depth of the tree by changing the value of the depth variable.

data.text/markdown: To layout the graph, we're going to preserve the shortest path distances between all pairs of nodes. The next cell computes these distances.

outputs.evalue: The variable 'shortest_paths_graph' was defined by another cell

data.text/markdown: To use an anchor constraint, we need the indices of the items we want to pin (remember that we will pin the leaves). We get the indices of the leaves using a simple formula.

outputs.evalue: The variable 'leaves' was defined by another cell

data.text/markdown: We want to pin the leaves to be uniformly spaced on a circle. The below cell constructs a Tensor in which the ith row holds the location to which the ith leaf should be pinned. If you like, you can try changing the radius to see what effect it has on the embedding.

outputs.evalue: The variable 'angles' was defined by another cell

data.text/markdown: Now that we have the leaves (the anchors) and the desired positions (their values), we can create the anchor constraint.

data.text/markdown:
Anchor Constraints

In this notebook, we show how to use an anchor constraint, which lets us pin some of the embedding vectors to specific values. This can be useful if you know a priori what some of the embedding vectors should be. Below, we'll use an anchor constraint when laying out a binary tree: we'll pin the leaves to lie on a circle.
This next cell constraints a binary tree with a specified depth. You can change the depth of the tree by changing the value of the depth variable.
To layout the graph, we're going to preserve the shortest path distances between all pairs of nodes. The next cell computes these distances.
To use an anchor constraint, we need the indices of the items we want to pin (remember that we will pin the leaves). We get the indices of the leaves using a simple formula.

We want to pin the leaves to be uniformly spaced on a circle. The below cell constructs a Tensor in which the ith row holds the location to which the ith leaf should be pinned. If you like, you can try changing the radius to see what effect it has on the embedding.
Now that we have the leaves (the anchors) and the desired positions (their values), we can create the anchor constraint.

We can now create the embedding. Feel free to play around with the distortion function (try changing it to pymde.losses.Quadratic, or pymde.losses.Cubic) to see what effect the choice of distortion function has on the emedding.
For fun, we can make a GIF of how the embedding was created, using the play method.
